notes: Liability-only trial on vicarious liability and insurance construction; Wilkie J's findings are detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Hawley v Luminar: door-steward assault, temporary deemed employment and public liability cover
key_facts: Door steward Geoffrey Warren, employed by ASE Security Services, punched customer David Hawley outside a Luminar Chicago Rock Café in Southend, causing severe brain and skull injuries.
Warren was convicted of inflicting grievous bodily harm; ASE entered default judgment and Luminar sought indemnity under its security contract.
Luminar's club management exercised detailed control over ASE stewards through contract, licence conditions and operational practice.
ASE's public liability policy covered accidental bodily injury, but the insurer argued deliberate assault by Warren was not accidental from the perpetrator's perspective.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court liability-only trial on vicarious liability and a Third Parties (Rights against Insurers) Act declaration after preliminary issues and Part 20 contribution proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Luminar was vicariously liable as Warren's temporary deemed employer; ASE's liability under the default judgment fell within public liability cover viewed from the assured's perspective, so the claimant was entitled to the declaration sought.
enrichment.ratio: Where a hirer exercises the Mersey Docks level of control over borrowed security staff, they become temporary deemed employers for vicarious liability notwithstanding contractual labels; in public liability insurance 'accidental bodily injury' is naturally construed from the assured's perspective and is not otiose because conduct may fall between deliberate wrongdoing and sudden unforeseen injury.
legal_issues: Whether Luminar was vicariously liable for Warren as a temporary deemed employee of ASE
Whether contractual indemnity and employment clauses could override factual control
Whether Hawley's injuries were accidental bodily injury under ASE's public liability policy
From whose perspective accidental bodily injury must be assessed

notes: Preliminary issue on unlawful-means conspiracy in carousel VAT fraud; Hodge J's analysis of cause of action is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Customs v Total Network: carousel VAT fraud and civil conspiracy preliminary issue
key_facts: HM Customs and Excise alleged Total Network SL, a Spanish mobile-phone trader, participated in thirteen carousel frauds in 2002 causing losses exceeding £1.9 million.
Transactions involved rapid chains of UK sales with a missing trader and fraudulent VAT repayment claims on goods exported zero-rated back to Spain.
The defendant was not a UK taxable person and had no direct VAT liability, but received purchase monies into UK bank accounts.
Proceedings were stayed for a preliminary issue on whether an unlawful-means conspiracy cause of action existed on assumed facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue trial on whether, as a matter of law, Customs had a cause of action in unlawful-means conspiracy as pleaded, on assumed facts of intentional revenue cheating.
enrichment.outcome: The preliminary issue was answered yes: fraud constituting cheating the public revenue could be unlawful means; the claim did not necessarily circumvent the VAT statutory scheme against a foreign non-taxable defendant.
enrichment.ratio: Unlawful-means conspiracy is not limited to injury to trade or business; fraud and cheating the revenue can constitute unlawful means even absent a direct civil wrong, and a civil conspiracy claim may lie against a foreign participant where statutory VAT recovery routes do not reach them.
legal_issues: Whether the conspiracy claim circumvented the statutory VAT recovery scheme
Whether cheating the public revenue amounted to unlawful means for conspiracy
Whether the tort requires harm to the claimant's trade or business
Whether a foreign non-taxable company could be sued outside VAT legislation

notes: Section 9 strikes clause appeal on Americanised Welsh Coal Charter; Teare QC's construction analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Frontier v Swissmarine: strikes clause and beyond control of consignee on demurrage
key_facts: Swissmarine chartered the CAPE EQUINOX to Frontier for a coal voyage from Australia to Mexico under an Americanised Welsh Coal Charter Form.
A Sicartsa employees' strike from 17 December 2001 to 16 January 2002 delayed discharge at Lazaro Cardenas.
Arbitrators awarded owners demurrage of US$236,763.51, holding a strike must be beyond the control of the consignee to interrupt laytime under clause 9.
Charterers amended clause 26 so they were liable for discharge demurrage though the clause still referred to the consignee.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court appeal from an arbitration award on the construction of a voyage charter strikes/demurrage clause, with permission granted on a point of general importance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the words 'beyond the control of the consignee' applied to strikes, lockouts and civil commotions as well as other causes, and the arbitrators' construction was correct.
enrichment.ratio: In a standard clause 9 strikes exception, the word 'other' extends 'beyond the control of the consignee' to specified events; laytime stops only where a strike both prevents or delays discharge and is beyond the consignee's control, even if charterers become liable for demurrage by amendment.
legal_issues: Whether 'beyond the control of the consignee' governed strikes as well as unspecified causes
Effect of amending clause 26 to make charterers liable for discharge demurrage
Whether the lockout and strikes exceptions were deprived of practical effect
Whether mitigation findings could uphold the award if construction were wrong

notes: State immunity and recognition of Danish ICC interim jurisdictional award; detailed arbitration Act analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Svenska Petroleum v Lithuania: state immunity and recognition of jurisdictional ICC award
key_facts: Svenska Petroleum sought to enforce a US$12.58 million ICC final award against Lithuania and Geonafta arising from a Lithuanian oilfield joint venture.
An interim award held Lithuania was party to the arbitration agreement, but Lithuania did not challenge it in Denmark before participating in a 13-day merits hearing.
Lithuania applied to set aside English enforcement proceedings claiming state immunity under section 9 of the 1978 Act.
Svenska applied to strike out the immunity challenge, arguing recognition of the interim award created issue estoppel on jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application to strike out or dismiss Lithuania's state immunity challenge, with preliminary questions on recognition of a New York Convention interim award and issue estoppel.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the court would exercise its section 103(2) discretion to recognise the interim award but the award was not final and conclusive under Danish law, so no issue estoppel arose.
enrichment.ratio: Section 73(2) principles may inform discretion under section 103(2) to recognise a foreign jurisdictional award where a state participated and lost but did not seek local review; however an arbitral ruling on jurisdiction is not final and conclusive for issue estoppel if Danish law permits court review when enforcement is sought.
legal_issues: Whether Lithuania waived state immunity by agreeing to arbitrate
Whether the interim award should be recognised under sections 101-103
Whether section 73(2) principles apply to Convention award recognition
Whether the interim jurisdictional award gave rise to issue estoppel

notes: IHT appeal on insolvent free estate and settled property aggregation; Re Barnes analysis applied.

enrichment.short_title: Green v HMRC: whether personal estate deficit reduces settled property for IHT
key_facts: The 12th Duke of Manchester died insolvent with about £4,600 of assets and liabilities exceeding assets by £44,671.
He held life interests in two settlements comprising securities worth about £50,594 and a house worth £290,000, treated as part of his estate under section 49.
Trustees claimed the free-estate deficit should reduce the value of the settled funds for inheritance tax.
HM Revenue and Customs refused the deduction and the trustees appealed the determination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 222 of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 against a Revenue determination on valuation of an aggregated death estate.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; personal liabilities could not reduce settled property value beyond exhausting the free estate net of liabilities answerable from it.
enrichment.ratio: Under sections 5(1) and 49 the deceased's estate is an aggregate of net property interests; section 5(3) requires liabilities to be taken into account by offsetting them only against assets liable to meet them, following Re Barnes, and excess personal debts cannot create a minus quantity against trust assets.
legal_issues: Whether section 5(3) operated on the aggregated estate including settled property
Whether personal liabilities could offset trust assets after the free estate was exhausted
How 'property' and 'estate' should be read consistently in sections 5 and 49
Whether Re Barnes remained applicable after the move to inheritance tax

notes: Ecstasy possession sentence appeal; short judgment reducing 18 months to 10 months.

enrichment.short_title: R v Orrin: reduction of ecstasy possession sentence from 18 to 10 months
key_facts: Steven Orrin pleaded guilty to possession of 32½ ecstasy tablets found in his jeans at a University of East Anglia disco.
He claimed the tablets were for personal use after buying 40 from a friend, with a history of drug-related convictions.
The recorder sentenced him to 18 months' imprisonment despite mitigation including employment and family concerns.
The court accepted custody was appropriate because of prior convictions and risk to other young people on university premises.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal sentence appeal by leave of the single judge after guilty plea at Norwich Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the sentence was reduced from 18 months to 10 months' imprisonment as excessive for possession without intent to supply.
enrichment.ratio: Even where ecstasy possession on university premises with prior convictions justifies custody, an 18-month term after guilty plea was outside the appropriate range and a term of about ten months better reflected the offence and mitigation.
legal_issues: Whether 18 months was manifestly excessive for possession of ecstasy for personal use
Appropriate sentencing range after guilty plea given prior convictions
Weight to be given to risk of tablets reaching other young people without a supply conviction

notes: Long TCC trial on TSKJ contracting identity and unpaid pipe-cleaning invoices at NLNG plant; final figures explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Tube Tech v TSKJ: consortium liability for unpaid LNG plant pipe-cleaning contracts
key_facts: Tube Tech cleaned condenser and heat exchanger pipework at Nigeria LNG's Bonny Island plant under contracts labelled TSKJ.
The TSKJ consortium comprised Technip, Snamprogetti, Kellogg and JGC, but defendants argued Tube Tech contracted only with a Madeiran fifth defendant.
Tube Tech claimed £643,295.11 unpaid across contracts 1, 2, 2A and 3; defendants counterclaimed for alleged under-manning.
Contracts were daily-rate service agreements with estimated prices, not open-ended cost-plus revaluation exercises.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of a commercial claim for unpaid invoices and counterclaims for breach of personnel conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Tube Tech for £538,791.67 plus interest against the first four defendants; claim against the fifth defendant and all counterclaims were dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: By acquiescing in use of the consortium name and signing as TSKJ, the first four defendants were liable on contracts 1 and 2; estimated daily-rate service contracts did not imply final revaluation by man-hours, and approximate staffing figures were not conditions precedent to payment.
legal_issues: Whether Tube Tech contracted with the TSKJ consortium or only the fifth defendant
Construction of estimated price and pro-rata clauses in contracts 1 and 2
Whether failure to deploy stated personnel numbers entitled defendants to withhold payment
Liability for consumables and unpaid invoices under contracts 2A and 3

notes: Undue influence appeal on transfer of half house for mortgage payment; Jacob LJ's Etridge analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Leeder v Stevens: undue influence in transfer of half house for £5,000 mortgage payment
key_facts: Defendant owned a Clevedon house worth about £70,000 with a £5,000 mortgage and agreed to transfer half to her long-term partner for his paying off the mortgage.
The claimant was a married man who did not live in the house; the draft deed allowed either party to force sale subject to pre-emption.
The defendant signed without independent legal advice after correspondence from the claimant's solicitor describing a straight £5,000 consideration.
District Judge Singleton rejected undue influence without resolving key factual conflicts and largely adopting the claimant's skeleton.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's appeal from a district judge's refusal to set aside a transfer on presumed undue influence under Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge principles.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the transaction was set aside on terms requiring repayment of about £30,000 representing the mortgage payoff and improvements with interest.
enrichment.ratio: Where a vulnerable cohabitee transfers half her home for grossly inadequate consideration in a relationship of trust, Etridge presumption applies even without overt coercion; knowing what she signed does not rebut the presumption, and inadequate judicial fact-finding on disputed evidence vitiates the decision.
legal_issues: Whether presumed undue influence arose under Etridge
Whether the transaction was manifestly disadvantageous and called for explanation
Whether lack of independent advice and solicitor's letter rebutted the presumption
Appropriate equitable remedy where some money was paid by the claimant

notes: Attorney General's reference on acid-throwing sentence; court declined to increase four-year term.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 119/2004: no increase of four-year sentence for pub acid attack
key_facts: The offender threw drain-cleaning sulphuric acid at a barman ejecting her from a Bristol pub, injuring 28 people including herself.
She pleaded guilty to section 18 GBH with intent and further section 20 and 47 offences with 23 similar assaults taken into consideration.
Three victims suffered really serious harm with permanent facial scarring; she had relevant prior convictions including hammer and bladed-article offences.
Recorder Stewart-Smith QC sentenced her to four years after early guilty pleas, mitigated by lack of premeditation and her own severe burns.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient sentence for corrosive-fluid assaults.
enrichment.outcome: Reference granted but court declined to interfere; although four years was lenient and possibly unduly lenient, double jeopardy and prison progress justified no increase.
enrichment.ratio: For a large-scale unpremeditated acid attack with many injured victims and serious prior violence, a four-year term after plea may be lenient yet not warrant appellate increase where the offender suffered grave self-inflicted injuries and was making constructive progress in custody.
legal_issues: Whether four years was unduly lenient for section 18 acid assault on multiple victims
Relevance of absence of premeditation and offender's own injuries
Application of double jeopardy discount on Attorney General references
Appropriate comparison with Grant, Radford and AG Ref No 3 of 2000

notes: Second appeal on CPR Part 36 reduction after undisclosed insurance payment mistake; Flynn v Scougall applied.

enrichment.short_title: Awberry v Marley: Part 36 reduction permitted after insurer mistake on benefits
key_facts: Employer Marley admitted liability for Awberry's workplace accident but disputed quantum of about £300,000.
Marley paid £189,218.72 into court under Part 36, which the claimant accepted before discovering a £55,362 personal accident insurance payment.
Marley applied to reduce the payment in court but the district judge refused, treating the issue as a change of mind rather than mistake.
The circuit judge allowed Marley's appeal, finding the district judge failed to weigh the injustice of holding the defendant to a 25% higher payment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from a circuit judge's decision allowing reduction of a Part 36 payment after acceptance, following Flynn v Scougall principles.
enrichment.outcome: Second appeal dismissed; the circuit judge was entitled to find the district judge's decision wrong for failing to give sufficient weight to a simple mistake about recoverable benefits.
enrichment.ratio: On a review appeal under CPR 52.11, a decision refusing permission to reduce a Part 36 payment may be wrong where the judge failed to consider or accord proper weight to the major injustice of enforcing a payment materially inflated by an undisclosed insurance receipt that arose from a simple mistake.
legal_issues: When CPR 36.6(5) permits reduction of a Part 36 payment after acceptance
Whether Flynn v Scougall change-of-circumstances test was satisfied
Proper approach to review appeals where the lower court failed to weigh a fundamental factor
Effect of a £55,362 personal accident policy payment on quantum
